rationale: Across published cohorts and systematic reviews of Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS), severe structural upper-limb reduction defects (transverse limb amputations, acheiria, oligodactyly, or forearm agenesis) are hallmarks restricted almost exclusively to classical CdLS caused by pathogenic variants in NIPBL. Pathogenic variants in BRD4 lead to CdLS type 6 (CDLS6), which presents as a milder, non-classic CdLS-like phenotype featuring subtle distal anomalies (e.g., small hands, clinodactyly) or normal limbs, but lacking severe congenital limb reduction defects. Kaur et al. (2023) and Selicorni et al. (2021) confirm that NIPBL remains the only established gene associated with severe classical limb reduction defects, and no confirmed cases of BRD4 variants with transverse limb amputations have been identified in the literature.

evidence.text: Variants in NIPBL account for the majority of CdLS cases and represent the only gene identified to date that results in the severe or classic form of CdLS with structural limb-reduction defects when mutated, whereas BRD4 variants cause a CdLS-like phenotype without classic severe reduction defects.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact prevalence of minor distal limb anomalies (e.g., clinodactyly, small hands, single palmar crease) in molecularly confirmed BRD4 patients compared to non-NIPBL cohesinopathy cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: While severe reduction defects discriminate NIPBL from BRD4, minor distal anomalies are reported across non-classic CdLS cases and require systematic phenotypic quantification to assess their utility in distinguishing BRD4 from HDAC8, SMC1A, or RAD21 cases.
